(Issue #439) By The Medium Blog (https://medium.com/blog?source=email-623e23a7d13f-1785327576071-newsletter.v3-15f753907972------------------------51598944_d940_4947_abe5_bc0dba22d566--------bf3f56c7deec) ∙ July 29, 2026 ∙ 6 min read ∙ View on Medium (https://medium.com/blog/fb08506a8d5c?source=email-623e23a7d13f-1785327576071-newsletter.v3-15f753907972------------------------51598944_d940_4947_abe5_bc0dba22d566--------bf3f56c7deec) Karola in her Studio by Dominik Skutetzky, via Wikimedia Commons (http://redirect.medium.systems/r-usThrrRnFV?source=email-623e23a7d13f-1785327576071-newsletter.v3-15f753907972-fb08506a8d5c-----------------------51598944_d940_4947_abe5_bc0dba22d566--------bf3f56c7deec) "History is written by the painter," writes Anna Saraiva (https://medium.com/u/94cc502e8bf5) in her analysis of Jacques Louis David (https://medium.com/@annasaraiva/jacques-louis-david-f003f9401c33) , the painter of Napoleon and countless other historical pieces of art. It's not just histories, though - context, culture, and emotions are all imbued into works of art. There are stories in the paint. On Medium, writers and publications are dedicated to exploring these hidden narratives. Let's take a look at three of them. ··· The Chess Game, which showed that female painters could attain both artistic competence and question social norms around gender, has been highlighted by scholars as having contributed to the foundation for subsequent feminist reappraisals of Renaissance art. One wonders why it took so long; it seemed pretty obvious to me when I looked at it today. - Marc Barham in Behind the Brushstrokes, 'The Game of Chess' (1555) by Sofonisba Anguissola ··· The hidden woman Mary and Child Surrounded by Seraphim and Cherubim, part of the Melun Diptych (1452–58) by Jean Fouquet, courtesy of Christopher P Jones (https://medium.com/u/d851bec3cba) There are thousands of medieval depictions of the Virgin Mary with a baby Jesus; what makes Jean Fouquet's 1458 depiction stand out? In One of the Strangest Paintings in Art History (http://redirect.medium.systems/r-pnptTAfxk9?source=email-623e23a7d13f-1785327576071-newsletter.v3-15f753907972-fb08506a8d5c-----------------------51598944_d940_4947_abe5_bc0dba22d566--------bf3f56c7deec) , writer Christopher P Jones (https://medium.com/u/d851bec3cba) explores how this painting features several traditional depictions of Madonna, including symbols of motherhood, monarchy, and heaven. But there's something off about this painting that has inspired debate art historians for centuries - "a flavour of blasphemous boldness," as historian Johan Huizinga wrote in 1919. It's thought that Fouquet's Mary is thought to resemble a mistress of his patron, King Charles VII of France: Her name was Agnès Sorel. As the king's favourite, she gave birth to three of his children, all of them girls. Originally a lady-in-waiting at court, she became the first officially acknowledged royal mistress in French history, and was credited with lifting the king out of a long depression and spurring him to action against English forces occupying French soil. At court, she is said to have generated scandal through her fashion, which included uncommonly low-cut dresses. The circumstances of her death are disputed, with some suggestion that she died of mercury poisoning shortly after giving birth to another of the king's offspring - perhaps dying at the hands of a rival. That the story might be a bit more complicated than a mistress hiding in plain sight. The painting was commissioned by "Étienne Chevalier, the treasurer to King Charles VII, and also the executor of Agnès Sorel's will," Jones writes; in fact, the painting is part of a pair that features Chevalier himself.
